title: Rainfall Deficits, Financial Protection, and Where Households Seek Care: Evidence from Four Rounds of the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel
content: Background. Climate variability is widely expected to raise the burden of illness in sub-Saharan Africa, but far less is known about what it does to the financing of care. A rainfall deficit arrives as an income shock in agrarian households at the same time as it may arrive as a health shock, and in a system financed overwhelmingly out of pocket those two events interact. Methods. We assembled an individual-level panel of 107,668 person-rounds drawn from 53,575 individuals in 8,518 households across all four rounds of the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel, covering 2010/11 to 2018/19 and 899 enumeration areas in 37 states. Rainfall at each household’s true coordinates, extracted before public displacement, was expressed as a proportional deviation from that location’s own long-run mean; a deficit is the bottom quintile of that deviation. Two-way fixed-effects models with household or individual effects and round effects, and standard errors clustered on the enumeration area, were estimated for reported morbidity, care-seeking, the source of care and out-of-pocket outlay measured against the SDG 3.8.2 thresholds. Information access was measured by household broadcast ownership and tested against a matched non-informational durable. Results. A rainfall deficit raised the probability that a household spent more than a tenth of its consumption out of pocket on health by 3.74 percentage points (95% CI 0.61 to 6.87) against a base of 14.3 percent, and the out-of-pocket budget share by 4.24 percentage points (95% CI 0.43 to 8.05). The effect was positive at every threshold between 1 and 40 percent of consumption and was concentrated in rural households (5.08 points, 95% CI 1.46 to 8.70). It survived correction for multiple testing within the financial-protection family (q = 0.039). Conditional on consulting, deficits moved care away from retail drug sellers and toward traditional and spiritual providers; the latter shift was confined to households without broadcast access, where it reached 3.51 points on a base of 6.8 percent and was fully offset among households with access (interaction −4.64 points, p = 0.028). Reported illness rose modestly and the decision to consult at all was unchanged. Conclusions. The dominant health consequence of a rainfall deficit in this setting is financial rather than clinical: households do not stop seeking care, they pay a larger share of a smaller budget for it and some of them change who they pay. Financial protection instruments that are responsive to agro-climatic conditions, and broadcast health communication in deficit-prone areas, address two distinct margins of the same shock.
